newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil on tenterhooks over re-election vote.
newsitem.headline: Brazil on tenterhooks over re-election vote.

text.p: Politicians broke from backroom negotiations over Brazil's re-election bill to return home on Friday, leaving newspapers to speculate as to the government's chances of holding a key vote on the issue next week.

In an upbeat briefing late on Thursday, presidential spokesman Sergio Amaral told reporters the government was confident it had enough votes to put re-election to a first of two Chamber of Deputies votes next week.

Government whips said 60 of the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party's (PMDB) 102 deputies would vote, giving them a total of 322 votes, more than the 308 needed for a three-fifths majority needed to approve the bill in the lower house.

Newspapers attributed the official optimism to tough words from President Fernando Henrique Cardoso who hinted he might banish the PMDB from his government if they continued to hold up the re-election bill.
But PMDB senators stuck firm to their insistence that the party must ignore the re-election bill until after elections for new presidents of the Senate and Chamber of Deputies on February 4.

The PMDB wants to prevent the government from backing a rival candidate in the Senate race. The government, however, fears voting on re-election would be risky in the wake of the hotly disputed congressional elections.
"From now until Tuesday, the air in Brasilia will be polluted with higher than normal levels of bluffs and lies," wrote Folha de Sao Paulo columnist Fernando Rodrigues.
"But the agony won't drag on. Next week everyone will have to show their cards. Whoever's bluffing will lose," he said.
Tereza Cruvinel, writing in daily O Globo, said Cardoso's game plan remained enigmatic.

"Never has Fernando Henrique been more sphinx-like, telling people only bits of what he thinks: to some, he will risk a vote on the 29th; to others, he still wants an agreement with the PMDB or that he favors a referendum or a plebiscite," she wrote.
In a scorching editorial, Jornal do Brasil lambasted the delaying tactics of the PMDB senators.

"No one can stand any more these specialists in paralysing Congress, sullying the government, tricking the media, irritating public opinion, slowing institutional improvement and blocking the movement of history," the editorial raged.
